prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting network learned to choose DONE before any placement, which suggests it cannot connect the target to the build. In this world the target channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, with wrap-around. The starting network looks only at single cells (1x1 stem), then two 3x3 convs, so it sees at most ±2 columns. It can never see the build at column x and its target at column x+4 together. Random placements then mostly earn negative reward, and DONE (reward 0) wins. The first job is to let the network learn this alignment without hard-coding the shift. A learned full-width convolution along each row, with circular padding, can reach any column offset, so it can learn the +4 offset on any grid. All three candidates use it. Candidates 1 and 2 differ only in recipe, and candidates 2 and 3 differ only in network.

### Round 2
The circular full-row stem is what made learning possible. It lets each cell line up the build at column x with the observed target channels at x+4 mod X, and it took dev success from 0 to about 0.40. Seed noise is very large: r1c2 scored 0.078 and 0.777. So r1c2 (0.428) and r1c1 (0.401) are effectively tied. There are two failure modes. One is collapse to DONE (r1c3 seed 0, and the starting architecture). The other is a mid-quality local optimum where the agent stops early (r1c2 seed 0: 7.6 placements, IoU 0.71). Adding global row and column mixing (r1c3) cost samples and collapsed on one seed. Its other seed reached 0.33, so it is not clearly worse. When training succeeds, capacity is clearly enough (0.78), so the main lever is more reliable training. This round tests three things on the r1c2 network: more samples (ppo_epochs 1), a longer horizon for the exact-build bonus, and small-gain output initialisation for a near-uniform starting policy.

### Round 3
The circular full-row stem solved the 4-column shift: every stem-only trial scores about 0.40–0.45. It sits in a two-way split by seed. Seed 1 reaches 0.68–0.87. Seed 0 either collapses to DONE (r2c1, r1c3) or reaches about 0.08. Recipe changes (1 or 2 epochs, gamma 0.99, small-gain init) are all within that noise. The seed-0 traces show what goes wrong: correct alignment, no cells placed outside the target, but it only ever fills layer 0 and then stops. It never stacks. Stacking needs a three-way conjunction: the target misses a cell at layer z, the build is empty at z, and z−1 is filled. The rolled target makes this harder. That points to two bottlenecks: perceiving stacking per layer, and a conservative early policy that exploration cannot escape. Global row and column mixing (r1c3) cost samples and failed.

### Round 4
Lining up the rolled target with the build is what unlocks learning. The starting network and every trial without circular row mixing collapsed to choosing DONE at once. Seed 0 is the bottleneck. It scored exactly 0.0781 in four different trials, so it reliably settles into a policy that fills layer 0 only and then stops. That suggests stacking is hard to perceive, because the conjunction 'build filled at z-1 here and target missing at z four columns away' must be learned inside one wide row conv. The recipe changes (more samples, a longer horizon, more entropy, small-gain initialisation) moved the mean by no more than seed noise. r1c1, with the default 4 epochs, had the most balanced seeds (0.31 / 0.49). The full-row and full-column trunk failed (seed 0 chose DONE immediately). The per-layer stem helped seed 0 only with entropy 0.04, and seed 1 fell at the same time. Final round: test a factorised alignment layer under two recipes, plus r1c1 with a long horizon.

## Trial it ended with
name: circular stem, long horizon
hypothesis: Same as r1c2 but with gamma 0.99 and gae_lambda 0.95. With gamma 0.95, the +1 exact-build bonus is discounted to about 0.6 by the time it reaches early placements. That weakens credit for build order (fill under overhangs before covering them) and for finishing instead of stopping early. A longer horizon should raise exact builds and placements per episode. Refuted if the mean is at or below 0.43, or if episodes still end early.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 1 states the rule directly: "In this world the target channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, with wrap-around." Round 2 says the same thing again: the stem lines up "the build at column x with the observed target channels at x+4 mod X." Together these give what changes (the target channels), how much (a 4-column shift toward higher x) and that it wraps around.
